docs.title: ats-strike
docs.text:
Turn a job description and your unstructured experiences into a tailored, two-page LaTeX CV and a cover letter, using any OpenAI-compatible model.

ats-strike is two halves that never share a machine by necessity:

  • a server that holds the model API keys, the prompts and the LaTeX toolchain, shipped as a container image;
  • a client that holds your CV data and your files, shipped as a single executable with no Python, no API key and no LaTeX of its own.

They speak HTTP, multipart/form-data in and JSON out, over a wire format both sides import and neither owns.

docs.title: The shape of a run
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    JD["a job posting<br/>(clipboard, folder or file)"] --> C["client<br/><i>your data, your files</i>"]
    C -->|HTTP| S["server<br/><i>models + pdflatex</i>"]
    S -->|"document · LaTeX · PDF · request ids"| C
    C --> OUT["cv/26-01-15/Acme_Corp_Head_of_IT/<br/>cv_you_head_of_it.pdf · .tex · .json<br/>analysis.json · jd.txt · log.log"]

Your profile, your contact details and your images travel with each request and are thrown away when it ends. The server keeps no database and no accounts — only a directory per request, holding that request's log and, for a CV job, its state and its result.

docs.title: The three packages
docs.text:
client/ The CLI. Watches your clipboard or a folder, keeps your CV data local, files every result in a dated folder. server/ The HTTP API. Writes the CV in six steps, validates it, compiles the PDF, analyses postings, writes letters. contracts/ The shapes both sides agree on — the one thing each side imports, so neither imports the other.

The short quickstarts live in the repository's README.md, client/README.md and server/README.md. These pages are the long form: what the system does, why it is built this way, and every parameter of both halves.

docs.title: What crosses the wire
docs.text:
Everything personal arrives with the request. The server has no database, no accounts and no seeded state; the only thing it keeps is a CV job's session, one directory of events:

$ATS_WORK_DIR/<session id>/events/
    000001.json   {"type": "status", "data": {...}}
    000002.json   {"type": "log", "data": {...}}
    000003.json   {"type": "usage", "data": {...}}
    000004.json   {"type": "artifact", "data": {...}}   a step's result
    ...
    000042.json   {"type": "result", "data": {...}}   the CV: the last event

Each event is its own file, written once and never changed — which is what a bucket mounted as a folder (OSS, Cloud Storage) can do: an object there cannot be appended to, and a rename is a copy. A reader lists the directory and reads what is new; the one file that may not read whole yet is the newest, so a reader stops there and finds it complete on its next look. The session id is the client's: the SHA-256 of the posting's text, so the same posting finds its session again. A session is deleted when the client acknowledges it, or once its last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS; a running one, never. The scratch directory a job compiles in is on local disk, and is gone with the job.

docs.title: Inside the server
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    REQ["request"] --> MW["RequestContextMiddleware<br/>assigns request_id, binds the Run"]
    MW --> AUTH{"ATS_API_TOKEN set?"}
    AUTH -->|"no match"| E401["401 unauthorized"]
    AUTH -->|"ok / not set"| PARTS["multipart parts<br/>size, UTF-8, JSON, ≤10 images"]
    PARTS --> SLOT{"a free job slot?"}
    SLOT -->|"no"| E429["429 too_many_jobs<br/>Retry-After: 30"]
    SLOT -->|"yes"| KIND{"which endpoint?"}
    KIND -->|"/v1/jd/*, /v1/letter, /v1/cv/render"| POOL["threadpool<br/>answer when done"]
    KIND -->|"/v1/cv"| THREAD["worker thread<br/>answer 202 now"]
    POOL --> ENV["Envelope<br/>its log: stdout"]
    THREAD --> EVENTS["an event per step, step result,<br/>log line and model call"]
    EVENTS --> STREAM["GET /v1/cv/{id}/events"]

POST /v1/cv for a session id that already has one skips the slot and the thread: it answers 202 with reattached: true, and the caller follows the events that are there.

  • One exception handler. describe_failure() is the single place that decides what an exception produces on the wire, so a failure body has the same shape as a success: a request_id, ok: false and one line naming the kind and the stage. See error model.
  • One semaphore. ATS_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS (10) bounds requests in flight. A full server refuses immediately rather than queueing a caller for minutes.
  • The pipeline is a library. Everything under pipeline/ takes its inputs in memory and returns its outputs; it reads no configuration, resolves no paths and writes nothing outside the scratch directory it is handed. That is what makes it safe to run per request.
  • The LaTeX subprocess is sandboxed. Shell escape off, reads and writes confined to the scratch directory, no stdin, a timeout, its own HOME and TEXMFVAR. A request may supply both the template and a whole .tex, so both are treated as hostile input.

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
One provider, one API key, one endpoint — declared once in the [provider] table of resources/models.toml. Every role calls it, except a role that sets use_alternate_provider = N (N ≥ 2), which calls provider N instead — the [provider] variable names with N appended (MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2 for 2):

Role Used for Shipped as detect JD detection: a one-word YES/NO on text that passed the free checks deepseek-v4.1-flash, thinking off, 1000 max output tokens, temperature 0 analysis JD analysis; searches the web for the company evaluation qwen3.8-flash, thinking on, max effort letter Cover letters; searches the web for the employer qwen3.8-flash, thinking on, max effort jd_evaluation A CV's first step: the JD's key points, each with an importance deepseek-flash on DeepSeek's API (provider 2), medium effort profile_scoring Each list of the profile scored against the key points the same, high effort format_selection The CV format, the experiences shown and their duty caps the same, medium effort cv Writing the CV body, and each experience on its own the same, medium effort validation Checking the body and each experience against the profile, as replace_in_* tool calls the same, medium effort highlight The **bold**/*italic* keyword pass over the validated CV the same, medium effort

See the CV pipeline for how the last six fit together.

Every call goes through cv_server.models: one LangChain chat model per role, built once at startup by the role's model_provider (standard, on ChatOpenAI, or deepseek, on ChatDeepSeek), and two methods. ModelSelector.call_llm(role, type, system_prompt, messages) returns the reply as a pydantic model, a bool (YES/NO), a str, or a JSON list or dict; call_tools(role, tool, …) returns the arguments of the tool calls the reply made. Both retry a reply that is empty, cut off or invalid — three calls in all, each retry told what was wrong. Provider-specific request fields (thinking_budget, enable_search) are the role's extra_body, sent as given: nothing checks a combination against what the endpoint supports. Any key of a role can be overridden with a ATS_<ROLE>_<FIELD> environment variable without editing the file; an empty value drops the key. A request can bring a <role>_extra_body for every role but detect, which supersedes all of that role's settings for that request.

Every pydantic reply is validated. Its schema reaches the model once: in the request with json_schema, in the system prompt with json_mode. A weak mode costs a retry, never correctness. The CV steps reply with JSON their prompts describe — the writer's two schemas are part of its input — and are parsed, not validated.

docs.title: Asynchrony, and why
docs.text:
Writing a CV takes minutes. POST /v1/cv answers 202 and hands the work to a plain thread that outlives the response; the thread reports itself by appending events to the session, and GET /v1/cv/{id}/events streams them — everything so far, then each new one, until the last. A stream is a reader of files, so it can be opened again at any time: after a dropped connection, with Last-Event-ID, to get what it missed; after a client crash, from the start. The client acknowledges the session (DELETE) only once the CV is stored.

The consequences are worth knowing before you deploy:

  • A running job lives in one instance. Its events are files, so any instance sharing the work root can replay them, but only the instance that started it is writing them. Run one instance.
  • WEB_CONCURRENCY=1. The slots and the workers are per-process, and a starting process ends every session that has not ended with a 503 error — correct for its own orphans, wrong for a sibling's live jobs.
  • A job cannot be cancelled yet. An abandoned one holds a slot until its own budget runs out (ATS_REQUEST_BUDGET_SECONDS, 20 minutes), and its session cannot be acknowledged until then.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Every response carries a request_id, and so does the X-Request-Id header. Every line the server logs to stdout carries it too.

A CV job streams its own account: every line it logged as a log event, every model call as a usage event with its duration and token counts, each step's result as an artifact event, and the run's total in its last event — failed attempts included, because they were paid for. The client writes the lines and the calls into log.log next to the CV, and each result into steps/. Nothing else rides on a reply: for a detection, an analysis, a letter or a render, the server's own log is where the commentary is.

docs.title: Building the client
docs.text:
The client ships as a single executable — no Python on the user's machine, no virtualenv, no install step.

uv sync
uv run --with pyinstaller pyinstaller --noconfirm client/packaging/cv.spec
./dist/cv --help
./dist/cv version

That produces dist/cv (or dist/cv.exe on Windows).

docs.title: What the spec does
docs.text:
client/packaging/cv.spec:

  • Entry point is client/packaging/entrypoint.py, not cv_client/__main__.py. PyInstaller runs its entry script as a top-level module, where __main__.py's relative import has no package to resolve against.
  • Bundled data: applications.xlsx, the empty spreadsheet copied on first use, and the package's own .dist-info via copy_metadata. cv version reads importlib.metadata, and a frozen application has no metadata unless it is copied in — without it the binary prints version unknown. Everything else the client needs — your profile, your template, your images — it reads from the folder you run it in at runtime, which is the whole point.
  • Excludes: fastapi, uvicorn, starlette, openai, jinja2, pypdf, cv_server, tkinter, pytest. None of them belong in a client; excluding them keeps the binary small if one is ever pulled in transitively. tests/test_architecture.py enforces the same rule at the source level, so a bad import fails the test suite before it reaches the build.

PyInstaller does not cross-compile. Build each binary on the OS it is for.

Why PyInstaller and not Cython: Cython compiles modules to C extensions but still needs an interpreter and a launcher around them, so it does not produce the single file this is for. Nuitka would, and is the fallback if start-up time or source opacity ever matters more than build simplicity.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph matrix["client job — one runner per OS"]
        direction TB
        U["uv sync --frozen"] --> CACHE["restore the PyInstaller<br/>analysis cache<br/><i>key: uv.lock + the spec</i>"]
        CACHE --> BUILD["pyinstaller cv.spec"]
        BUILD --> HELP["./dist/cv --help<br/>./dist/cv version"]
        HELP --> SMOKE["Linux only:<br/>start ats-strike from source,<br/>render smoke.tex through it,<br/>assert the file starts with %PDF"]
        SMOKE --> ART["upload-artifact<br/>the bare binary"]
    end

The smoke test is the part worth keeping: --help proves the binary starts, but the real question is whether it talks to a server. render is the one call that needs no model, so CI starts the server from the same checkout with an invalid provider endpoint, renders a two-line .tex through the real multipart → envelope → pdflatex → base64 path, and checks the bytes on disk.

The analysis cache is keyed on uv.lock and the spec, because either one invalidates it; without it PyInstaller re-analyses every dependency from scratch on each run.

docs.title: What a user downloads
docs.text: A release is one flat .tar.gz holding both binaries and the files the client looks for by name. How it is assembled, and how to cut one, is in Cutting a release.

docs.title: Running from source instead
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run cv --help
uv run cv --server http://localhost:8080 clipboard --out ~/applications
uv run pytest client/tests        # no server, no terminal, no network

The client's tests fake at the boundary: CVApi is a protocol, so the modes run against a stub with no HTTP at all, and tests/test_integration.py drives the real client against the real app in-process through an httpx.Client — both halves, no socket.

docs.title: Adding a new way to feed it postings
docs.text: A source of job descriptions is a JDSource (client/src/cv_client/stages/listener.py): one method, poll(), that returns the next new text or None. The clipboard is one; a second — an IMAP folder, a browser extension, a queue — is a new file under client/src/cv_client/sources/, a thin mode that hands it to a Listener, and no change to the stages at all. watch and submit are not sources: watch reads its folder with its own inbox stage, and submit takes one file and runs the same stages once.

docs.title: Building the server
docs.text: The server is a container image: a Python virtualenv, the LaTeX toolchain and uvicorn. It mounts nothing and seeds nothing.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
cd <repo root>
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build -t ats-strike-server .

The Dockerfile lives at the repository root, not in server/, because some cloud builders refuse a Dockerfile in a subfolder. The build context is the root: the image needs contracts/ and server/, and nothing else.

Classic builder only. No BuildKit features and no heredocs — CI builds with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 on purpose, and the image must stay buildable that way.

flowchart TB
    subgraph s1["stage 1 — build (uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim)"]
        L1["pyproject.toml · uv.lock<br/>+ the three member pyprojects"] --> L2["uv sync --frozen --no-dev<br/>--package ats-strike-server<br/>--no-install-workspace"]
        L2 --> L3["contracts/src · server/src · server/resources"]
        L3 --> L4["uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-editable<br/>→ /app/.venv"]
    end
    subgraph s2["stage 2 — runtime (python:3.12-slim-bookworm)"]
        R1["texlive-latex-base + texlive-fonts-recommended + cm-super"] --> R2["vendored fontawesome5<br/>→ TEXMFLOCAL"]
        R2 --> R3["COPY --from=build /app/.venv"]
        R3 --> R4["entrypoint.sh → ats-strike"]
    end
    L4 --> R3

Why the layers are in that order: the lock file changes rarely and the code changes every commit, so dependencies resolve in a layer of their own. --no-editable copies the packages into the venv instead of linking them back to /app/src, so the runtime stage needs nothing but the venv.

docs.title: What the LaTeX bits are for
docs.text:
Package Why texlive-latex-base hyperref, graphicx, array, hhline, amsmath, babel-english — everything resume.tex.jinja uses texlive-fonts-recommended The font files behind psnfss (Charter, Times, Palatino, ...). The stock template does not need them; a template of your own that loads \usepackage{charter} does cm-super Type 1 CM fonts. Without them, T1 encoding falls back to bitmap fonts and the PDF looks scanned. cm-super-minimal is not enough: it leaves the design sizes the CV uses for headings and small print as Type 3 bitmaps fontawesome5 (vendored) The contact icons in the CV header. Debian ships it only inside the 1.7 GB texlive-fonts-extra, so it is vendored as a TeX Live archive in server/docker/vendor/ and unpacked into TEXMFLOCAL. No network access during the build

The image is ~780 MB, almost all of it that toolchain.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ats-strike-server
curl localhost:8080/healthz          # expect "pdflatex": true

It runs as any uid (--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"), needs no volume, and works with a read-only root filesystem as long as /tmp is writable and executable:

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:exec -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ats-strike-server

exec on that tmpfs is required: pdflatex writes and then reads back its font cache there. A tmpfs also means a CV session does not survive a restart — mount a volume, or a bucket, at ATS_WORK_DIR if you want it to.

server/compose.yaml does all of the above with the settings already wired:

cp .env.example .env     # then fill in one provider's API key
cd server && docker compose up --build

The published image is on Docker Hub:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -e MODEL_API_KEY=... \
  -e MODEL_API_KEY2=... -e MODEL_BASE_URL2=https://api.deepseek.com lmstch/ats-strike:latest

:latest and :x.y.z are pushed by the release workflow, not by hand — see Cutting a release. Pin the version tag if you want the server to stay where the client you handed out expects it.

docs.title: The provider
docs.text:
Three model roles, one provider, one API key. The endpoint is declared once in the [provider] table of resources/models.toml; the key comes from the environment.

MODEL_API_KEY=sk-...
MODEL_BASE_URL=https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works — OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, a local Ollama. Switching providers is replacing those two values; models.toml names the same two variables and does not need to change.

A model that sets use_alternate_provider = 2 calls a second endpoint, from MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2, instead; 3 uses MODEL_API_KEY3 / MODEL_BASE_URL3, and so on. The shipped six CV steps all use 2, DeepSeek's own API (https://api.deepseek.com): the server builds every role at startup and does not start without those two.

Per-role overrides need no rebuild either — ATS_<ROLE>_<FIELD>, for any key of a role, for DETECT, ANALYSIS, LETTER, JD_EVALUATION, PROFILE_SCORING, FORMAT_SELECTION, CV, VALIDATION and HIGHLIGHT:

ATS_CV_MODEL=qwen-max
ATS_CV_TEMPERATURE=0.2
ATS_CV_THINKING=off            # auto | on | off
ATS_CV_REASONING_EFFORT=high   # any string the provider accepts
ATS_CV_API=responses           # chat_completions | responses
ATS_CV_MODEL_PROVIDER=deepseek # standard | deepseek
ATS_CV_EXTRA_BODY={"thinking_budget": 4000}   # JSON; replaces the whole table
ATS_CV_USE_ALTERNATE_PROVIDER=2  # MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2
ATS_LETTER_TEMPERATURE=        # empty sends no temperature (OpenAI's reasoning models reject one)
ATS_LETTER_EXTRA_BODY={}       # no enable_search, for an endpoint without DashScope's

Nothing checks a combination against what the endpoint supports: what a role declares is what is sent. The comments in models.toml list the known traps.

docs.title: Prompts and the template
docs.text:
The five prompts and resume.tex.jinja ship inside the image. To change them permanently, mount a directory with your versions and set ATS_RESOURCES; anything missing there falls back to the built-in copy. To change them for one request, upload them as parts — that is what the client does when it finds them next to its executable.

docker run -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env \
  -v "$PWD/my-resources:/resources:ro" -e ATS_RESOURCES=/resources \
  ats-strike-server

docs.title: From a checkout
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run ats-strike            # http://localhost:8080
uv run pytest server/tests      # no API key, no network
uv run pytest                   # every package, plus the integration test

The LaTeX-dependent tests skip themselves when pdflatex is absent. Nothing in the suite calls a model: server/tests/server_helpers.py wires a real ModelSelector to a fake HTTP transport, so request assembly, structured output, retries and usage logging are all the production code paths. server/tests/golden/cv_golden.tex pins the whole render — an escaping regression is otherwise invisible until someone reads a bad PDF.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
A CV job runs for minutes after the request that started it has been answered. That is the one thing to plan around.

  • ATS_WORK_DIR is state. Every CV session lives there until the client acknowledges it, or until its last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS. The default is the system temp directory, which on most container platforms is RAM-backed and empty again after a redeploy. Mount a volume — or a bucket, as server/terraform does on Alibaba Cloud — to have sessions outlive the instance. Each event is a file written once, which a bucket mounted as a folder can do.
  • One process per work root. The job slots and the worker threads are per-process, and a starting process ends every session that has not ended with a 503 — right for its own orphans, wrong for a sibling's live jobs.
  • A CV's stream lasts as long as its job. Every other call returns in seconds; only /v1/cv/render waits on a compile. A platform request timeout has to outlast ATS_REQUEST_BUDGET_SECONDS plus the round in flight; the client reconnects after a cut, but some platforms restart the instance on a timeout.
  • Size for the compiles, not the waiting. Ten jobs in flight is the default; each is mostly idle on the provider — up to ten calls at once, for the steps that score or write one item each — but each also compiles LaTeX once, or a few times when it has to be trimmed.
  • Scaling. A running job lives in the instance that started it: run one instance.
  • Cold starts build an HTTP client per model role and read the prompts. Fast — but the first request also warms the LaTeX font cache in /tmp.

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text: A request may supply the LaTeX template, and /v1/cv/render accepts a whole .tex. That is arbitrary LaTeX, so every compile runs with shell escape disabled (-no-shell-escape, shell_escape=f), reads and writes confined to the scratch directory (openin_any=p, openout_any=p), no stdin to block on, a timeout, and its own HOME/TEXMFVAR. The scratch directory is deleted when the request ends, and the scratch path is scrubbed out of any LaTeX log that goes back to a client.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml has three jobs. The image one builds with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0, starts the container with a deliberately invalid provider endpoint, and asserts /healthz reports "pdflatex":true — the image is checked for the toolchain, not for a model.

.github/workflows/release.yml builds it the same way — classic builder, linux/amd64 — and adds one assertion before it pushes: that /healthz reports the version being released. The server reads its version from the installed package metadata, which the image builds with --no-editable, so that check is what proves the number on the Docker Hub tag is the number the container will report.

docs.title: The client
docs.text:
One executable, eight modes. It keeps your CV data on your machine and sends it, per request, to a server that holds the model API keys and the LaTeX toolchain. No Python, no API key and no LaTeX install of your own.

cv [global options] MODE [mode options]

Global options work on either side of the mode name: cv -v submit posting.txt --out ~/applications and cv submit -v … do the same thing.

docs.title: clipboard — copy a posting, get a CV
docs.text:
cv clipboard --out ~/applications

Watches the clipboard. When you copy something that looks like a posting, it checks with the server, analyses it, prints the analysis and asks — every posting, whatever its should_apply says:

Paste the posting URL to submit, y = submit without link, n/s = skip, q = quit
> https://jobs.example.com/12345
  • y, or the posting URL: its CV is queued and the clipboard is watched again at once. CVs are written in the background, one at a time, while you read the next posting; their lines are tagged with the job's folder name ([Acme_Corp_Head_of_IT] …) and held back while a question is on screen. The URL is stored in analysis.json and goes to the spreadsheet.
  • n or s: it is filed under discarded/.
  • q: clipboard mode stops. The posting stays in working/, marked PENDING in its approval_status.txt, and is asked about again at the next start — never decided by its should_apply.

Stopping. q also works while nothing is being asked: the CV being written is finished, and the approved ones still queued wait in working/ for the next start. Ctrl-C stops at once.

Startup. Anything left in working/ by a previous run is offered back to you first: resume, clean or quit. Resume sends each folder where its own files say — the table under watch's Startup: approved ones go straight to the CV writer, and the ones still waiting for an answer are asked about before anything new is read.

With --yes nothing is asked: every posting is submitted, and so is every leftover waiting for an answer.

On Linux the clipboard needs a helper — apt install xclip (X11) or wl-clipboard (Wayland) — and a reachable DISPLAY/WAYLAND_DISPLAY. The client probes it at startup and tells you if it cannot read it, instead of waiting forever for a change that can never arrive. Over SSH, forward X11 or use watch, which needs no clipboard at all.

docs.title: watch — drop files into a folder
docs.text:
cv watch --in ~/Downloads/postings --out ~/applications

Each posting goes through four stages, and the analysis decides the route: should_apply YES gets its CV without a question, CHECK waits for you, NO is put aside. The CVs are written in the background, one at a time, while you read the next posting.

flowchart LR
    IN["<b>1 · analysis</b><br/>--in"] -->|"YES"| GEN["<b>3 · waiting for the CV</b><br/>working/"]
    IN -->|"CHECK"| ASK["<b>2 · waiting for you</b><br/>working/"]
    IN -->|"NO"| DISC["discarded/"]
    IN -->|"not a posting,<br/>or a call failed"| ERR["error/"]
    ASK -->|"y"| GEN
    ASK -->|"d"| DISC
    ASK -->|"s / n: later"| ASK
    GEN -->|"written"| CV["cv/"]
    GEN -->|"a call failed"| ERR

What you can drop:

  • A .txt file — the posting, read as UTF-8 text. It has to look like a posting (the local check, then the server's), otherwise it lands in error/ with a .log beside it. Once its analysis is filed, the file is deleted from --in. Any other file — a PDF, a .docx — goes to error/ with nothing sent: paste its text into a .txt.
  • A folder holding jd.txt and a valid analysis.json — one from cv/, discarded/ or error/, for instance. Detection and analysis are skipped: it is copied into working/ under its company and title, removed from --in, and goes where its own files say (the table under Startup). One that also holds its CV (cv_<name>_<job_title>.json or a .tex) is re-rendered — one LaTeX compile, no model call, no new spreadsheet row. A folder with no jd.txt, or whose analysis.json does not validate, goes to error/ with a log.log inside saying why.

Names starting with . are ignored, and anything still being copied in is left alone until it stops changing.

When a posting needs you (CHECK), you see its text, then the analysis, and answer:

y = write the CV (or paste the posting URL), d = discard, s/n = next, q = quit
> https://jobs.example.com/12345
  • y, or the posting URL: its CV is queued. The URL is stored in analysis.json and goes to the spreadsheet.
  • d: it is filed under discarded/.
  • s or n: it is asked again after the others.

Your answer is kept in the folder as approval_status.txt — APPROVED or DISCARDED (clipboard and submit also write PENDING while they wait for yours). Anything typed before a posting was on screen is thrown away, so a stray y never approves one you have not read, and what the inbox and the CV writer print is held back until you have answered.

Stopping. q works at any time, also when nothing is waiting for you: nothing new is started, the posting being analysed and the CV being written are finished, then the watcher exits. Ctrl-C stops at once; the next start picks up whatever was running, and a posting still in --in is read again.

--yes asks nothing: YES postings get their CV, NO postings are discarded, and CHECK postings wait in working/ for a run without --yes.

Startup. Whatever an earlier run left in working/ goes where its own files say, before anything new is read. The rules are tried in this order:

The folder holds It goes to no jd.txt, or no valid analysis.json error/ its CV: cv_<name>_<job_title>.json or a .tex re-rendered, then cv/ no approval_status.txt by should_apply: YES to the CV queue, CHECK to you, NO to discarded/ approval_status.txt saying APPROVED the CV queue approval_status.txt saying DISCARDED discarded/ approval_status.txt saying PENDING you: asked about again, whatever should_apply says approval_status.txt saying anything else error/

A folder dropped into --in follows the same table. To retry a job that failed, move its folder from error/ back into --in; to have a CHECK posting written without being asked, set its approval_status.txt to APPROVED first. A loose file left in working/ by an older version goes to error/: move it back into --in to have it read again.

--in defaults to ./incoming, created if missing. It may not be the same folder as --out, and the watcher has to be allowed to delete from it.

docs.title: submit — one file, once
docs.text:
cv submit posting.txt --out ~/applications --yes

The same steps as clipboard, for a single file: analysed, asked about (unless --yes), and the CV written right there — the command returns once it is filed. No recovery prompt: a one-off run must not start by asking about someone else's leftovers. The file you name is read, never moved — unlike watch, which empties the folder it watches. q at the question leaves the posting in working/ as PENDING, to be asked about at the next start of clipboard or watch.

cv submit posting.txt analysis.json --out ~/applications

With an analysis.json for the posting — from an earlier run's folder, say — detection and analysis are skipped and it goes straight to the CV; you are still asked first, unless --yes. Both are copied into the job folder as jd.txt and analysis.json, so the analysis you passed is the one delivered beside the CV. One that does not validate stops the command before anything is sent or written.

docs.title: submit-raw — just the CV, right here
docs.text:
cv submit-raw posting.txt
cv submit-raw posting.txt -o cv.pdf -o cv.json -o cv.tex

The CV and nothing else: no detection, no analysis, no question before spending, no cover letter, no spreadsheet, no folders. Files land in the directory you are standing in.

-o is repeatable and the suffix is the whole instruction — .pdf writes the PDF, .json the document, .tex the LaTeX. A name you chose is overwritten without asking, because a name you chose is a name you meant. With no -o you get one PDF named after the posting (posting.txt → posting.pdf), and a second run counts up to posting_1.pdf rather than replacing it.

docs.title: analysis — just the analysis
docs.text:
cv analysis --in posting.txt
cv analysis --in posting.txt --output-format folder

The analysis and nothing else: no detection, no question, no CV. It needs candidate_profile.json and candidate_preferences.md, and costs one model call. With --output-format json (the default) the analysis is printed on stdout — nothing else is, so it pipes straight into jq. With folder it writes <Company>_<Title>/ holding jd.txt and analysis.json into --out, which defaults to incoming/ under --data-dir (or the current folder): the shape watch takes from its input folder, and the folder it watches by default. A folder of the same name is replaced. It is written as .<Company>_<Title>/ and renamed once both files are in, so a watch running on it never picks up half a job. Failures go to stderr.

docs.title: render — compile an edited CV
docs.text:
cv render ~/applications/cv/26-01-15/Acme_Head_of_IT/cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.json
cv render cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.tex --output /tmp/preview.pdf

Give it the .json document to re-render from the content, or the .tex to compile a hand-edit. The PDF lands next to the input unless --output says otherwise. Needs no profile and no posting — just the server — and costs one LaTeX compile and no model call. A failed render prints the end of the TeX log, which says where the LaTeX breaks.

docs.title: reset — drop what the server keeps
docs.text:
cv reset

Every CV is a session on the server, kept until the client has saved its files (see A CV that was interrupted). reset deletes every session the server still has — except one whose CV is still being written — and says how many it deleted. After it, every posting is written from scratch.

docs.title: version — which build is this
docs.text:
cv version

Prints version x.y.z and exits. It reads no configuration and talks to no server, so it answers even when cv.toml is wrong. Every --verbose run prints the same line at startup, which is what you want in a bug report.

The number comes from the package metadata bundled into the executable, so it is the version the release workflow built — there is no string in the source to forget to bump.

docs.title: Postings you have seen before
docs.text:
Before anything is spent on a posting, every analysis.json under cv/, discarded/ and working/ is read back. A posting is the same job when its URL matches, or when its company and title match — case, accents and spacing ignored. A side without a URL is compared by company and title only; one without a company or title, by URL only. Old files are read as they are, never validated: one that cannot be read is skipped.

The check runs as soon as a posting is analysed, before you are asked, in every mode. A posting already applied to, discarded or still in flight prints already applied, already discarded or already in progress with the earlier folder, and is dropped: nothing is asked and nothing is written. The mode carries on: the clipboard keeps waiting, submit exits. In watch, a posting with a JOB_POSTING: <url> line is checked by that URL before anything is sent, LinkedIn ids included: one already known is deleted from the inbox with the same message, and costs no call at all.

A posting that is dropped leaves nothing behind: the earlier copy already holds it. So to redo one, move the earlier folder out of cv/ or discarded/ first — before you copy the posting again, and instead of copying a folder you drop back into watch.

docs.title: A CV that was interrupted
docs.text:
A CV is a session on the server, named after the posting's text. While the CV is written the client follows it, printing each step, what each model call cost and the total at the end; once the files are saved, the client tells the server, which deletes the session. Anything in between costs nothing:

  • A dropped connection is picked up again on its own, from the last thing received.
  • A client that died — a closed laptop, Ctrl-C, a crash: run the same posting again, with submit, submit-raw, clipboard or watch, and the server replays the run from the start, still going or already finished, instead of writing a new CV. ↺ this posting already has a run on the server says so.
  • --new drops that run and writes the CV again: for when you changed your profile, your template, a prompt or an [extra_body], none of which change the posting's text. It is refused while the old run is still being written.

A session nobody came back for is kept for a day (the server's ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS), and cv reset drops them all.

docs.title: Global
docs.text: Flag What it does --server URL The ats-strike server. Default http://localhost:8080. --token TOKEN Bearer token, if the server requires one. --pages N Page limit the CV must fit. Default: the server's, which is 2. --config FILE Use this cv.toml instead of searching for one. --data-dir DIR Look for your files here before the current folder. -v, --verbose Print version x.y.z at startup, then what the server reports about each finished step — what it produced, tokens, thinking tokens, elapsed — plus the CV's session id and the /healthz attempts.

docs.text:
Flag Modes What it does --out DIR clipboard, watch, submit The output folder (working/, error/, discarded/, cv/). Default: the current folder. --in DIR watch The folder to watch. Default: ./incoming, created if missing. --in FILE analysis The posting to analyse. Required. --output-format json\|folder analysis json: print the analysis on stdout. folder: write <Company>_<Title>/ with jd.txt and analysis.json into --out, replacing one of the same name. Default json. --out DIR analysis Where --output-format folder writes. Default: <data-dir>/incoming, created if missing. --cover-letter no\|yes\|letter_only clipboard, watch, submit Also write a cover letter, or write only one. Default no. --yes clipboard, watch, submit Submit every valid posting without asking. Unattended runs spend tokens on their own. A posting already applied to, discarded or in flight is skipped, still without asking. In watch it only stops the questions: YES postings get their CV, NO postings are discarded, CHECK postings wait in working/ for a run without --yes. --no-xlsx clipboard, watch, submit Do not record delivered CVs in the spreadsheet. --new clipboard, watch, submit, submit-raw Write each CV again even when the server still has a run for the same posting, which is otherwise replayed. Exit code is 0 when nothing failed, 1 when a posting failed or the client could not start (a missing file, an unreachable server, a bad config).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Everything resolves in this order:

flowchart LR
    CLI["command line"] --> ENV["environment"] --> TOML["cv.toml"] --> FOUND["a file in the<br/>current folder"] --> SRV["the server's default"]

docs.title: cv.toml
docs.text:
Looked for as --config, then $ATS_CONFIG, then cv.toml in the current folder.

server_url   = "https://ats-strike.example.run.app"
token        = "the-bearer-token"   # only if the server requires one
cover_letter = "no"                 # no | yes | letter_only
# pages       = 2                   # page limit the CV must fit
# timeout     = 1800                # seconds to follow one CV job
# verbose     = true                # same as -v on every run

[files]                             # explicit paths win over discovery
# profile        = "~/cv/candidate_profile.json"
# candidate_data = "~/cv/candidate_data.json"
# preferences    = "~/cv/candidate_preferences.md"
# template       = "~/cv/resume.tex.jinja"
# prompt_jd_evaluation     = "~/cv/sys_prompt_jd_evaluation.txt"
# prompt_profile_scoring   = "~/cv/sys_prompt_profile_scoring.txt"
# prompt_format_selection  = "~/cv/sys_prompt_format_selection.txt"
# prompt_cv_body           = "~/cv/sys_prompt_cv_body.txt"
# schema_cv_body           = "~/cv/cv_body_schema.json"
# prompt_cv_duties         = "~/cv/sys_prompt_cv_duties.txt"
# schema_cv_duties         = "~/cv/cv_duties_schema.json"
# prompt_validation_body   = "~/cv/sys_prompt_validation_body.txt"
# prompt_validation_duties = "~/cv/sys_prompt_validation_duties.txt"
# prompt_highlight         = "~/cv/sys_prompt_highlight.txt"
# prompt_letter            = "~/cv/sys_prompt_letter.txt"
# prompt_analysis          = "~/cv/sys_prompt_analysis.txt"

# [extra_body.cv]                   # a role's settings, instead of all the server's
# temperature = 0.4

A relative path under [files] is resolved against the config file's own folder, and a path that does not exist is an error rather than a silent fallback. The keys are short on purpose: TOML reads candidate_profile.json = "x" as a dotted key, which is not what anyone means.

[extra_body.<role>] is what one model role runs on instead of the server's models.toml settings — all of them, not just the keys you set: what the table holds is sent into the request as is (temperature, top_p, reasoning_effort, a provider's own fields), with the model and the messages. The roles are the CV's six steps — jd_evaluation, profile_scoring, format_selection, cv, validation, highlight — and analysis and letter. Every table goes with every request, and each endpoint reads its own; a role the server does not have is ignored. An empty table sends an empty object: that role then runs with no settings at all.

docs.text: Variable What it does ATS_API_URL The server URL. Beaten by --server. ATS_API_TOKEN The bearer token. Beaten by --token. ATS_CONFIG Path to cv.toml. Beaten by --config.

docs.title: Your files
docs.text:
Put them in the folder you run from (or in --data-dir) and they are picked up by name:

File What it is Required candidate_profile.json Everything you have ever done. The models tailor the CV from this — the more complete, the better. Its experiences each need an id and duties. yes candidate_data.json Name, email, phone, LinkedIn, languages, location, education. Printed by the template as-is; no model is shown it. yes candidate_preferences.md What you want from a job, in prose. Scored against each posting. for analysis resume.tex.jinja Your own LaTeX template. no — the server's is used sys_prompt_jd_evaluation.txt, sys_prompt_profile_scoring.txt, sys_prompt_format_selection.txt, sys_prompt_cv_body.txt, sys_prompt_cv_duties.txt, sys_prompt_validation_body.txt, sys_prompt_validation_duties.txt, sys_prompt_highlight.txt, sys_prompt_letter.txt, sys_prompt_analysis.txt Your own prompts. no — same cv_body_schema.json, cv_duties_schema.json Your own JSON schemas for the CV body and for an experience: the writer is shown them, so a field you add here and in your template reaches the page. no — same

Every .png, .jpg and .jpeg in those folders is sent too, under its own file name — and that name is the whole contract: the server writes each one next to the .tex, so \includegraphics{photo.jpg} in your template is satisfied by a photo.jpg sitting next to you. At most 10 per request. candidate_signature.png is just one such image: the stock template includes it, and the server has a blank one if you do not.

Start from the fictional set in the repository's examples/candidate/.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
~/applications/
├── cv/
│   └── 26-01-15/
│       └── Acme_Corp_Head_of_IT/
│           ├── cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.pdf     the CV
│           ├── cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.tex     the LaTeX it was compiled from
│           ├── cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.json    the content, for re-rendering
│           ├── candidate_signature.png  the images your template includes
│           ├── analysis.json            match score, salary, skills, gaps
│           ├── jd.txt                   the posting, whatever the file was called
│           ├── cover_letter.txt         with --cover-letter
│           ├── steps/                   each step's result, as JSON: key_points.json, scored_profile.json, …
│           └── log.log                  every step, and the server's own lines for the CV
├── discarded/26-01-15/…                 postings you said no to, analysis kept
├── error/26-01-15/…                     rejected or failed, with a .log beside it
├── working/                             in flight, or waiting for you
└── applications.xlsx                    one row per delivered CV

File names come from your own candidate_data.json, not from the server.

To revise a CV: edit cv_jordan_rivera_head_of_it.json and run cv render on it — one LaTeX compile, no model calls. Editing the .tex and rendering that works too. The spreadsheet's own header row is the schema: rename, reorder or add columns in your copy and the rows follow.

log.log holds the client's steps, and every line the server logged while it wrote the CV, indented under them, as they streamed in:

2026-01-15T09:30:12 ✍ writing the CV (this takes minutes)...
2026-01-15T09:30:12    jd_evaluation
  2026-01-15T09:30:33+00:00 INFO    [cv.jd_evaluation]   ⏱ [jd_evaluation] deepseek-flash 21.2s | input=1847, thinking=7256, output=832, …
2026-01-15T09:30:33    ⏱ jd_evaluation deepseek-flash 21.2s | input=1847, thinking=7256, output=832
2026-01-15T09:30:33    profile_scoring
…
2026-01-15T09:35:24    Σ 21 model call(s), 961.4s | input=64148, thinking=161200, output=14091

One line per model call is what it cost, and the Σ line is the whole run — failed attempts included. The steps that make several calls make them at once, so the calls' seconds add up to more than the run took.

steps/ holds what each step handed the next one, as the server streamed it: the posting's key points, your profile with its scores and the evidence for them, the format chosen and why, the CV before and after validation, and the highlighted CV. A CV that failed half-way keeps the steps it finished, under error/. Only the final PDF is ever downloaded.

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text:
Per request: the posting text, your candidate_profile.json, your candidate_preferences.md (for the analysis), your candidate_data.json and every image in the folder. Whether the model provider keeps what it is shown is between you and whoever runs the server — the same question as with any hosted model.

No model is ever shown your candidate_data.json. It is sent because the server compiles the CV to count its pages, and a page count taken with the contact block missing is not the page count of the CV you will send; it goes to the LaTeX template and nowhere else.

Nothing at all is sent for text that fails the local length and binary checks, so a copied password or a screenful of code never leaves the machine. The server keeps a CV's session — what the job logged and the finished CV — until the client has saved the files, or for a day at most, and keeps nothing else.

flowchart LR

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1 — The free check runs on your machine. static_jd_guess lives in contracts/ precisely so both sides run the same one: the client uses it before spending a network call, the server before spending a model call. Copying a password or a line of code never reaches the network, and the terminal says so: [clipboard] ✗ not a job description (412 chars, nothing sent).

2 — /healthz before the first real call. A freshly started server (a cold container, a scale-to-zero platform) can take a moment to answer, so the client knocks up to three times, two seconds apart, once per process — not once per call. With -v it narrates the attempts.

3 — Detection costs one small model call. POST /v1/jd/detect answers {"is_job_description": true|false}. Why something was rejected is in the server's log for that request, not in the answer — a caller only ever branches on the verdict. A false verdict on a posting you wanted usually means the copy grabbed only part of the page.

4 — Analysis creates the folder, unless the posting was seen before. The company name and job title in the JDAnalysis are what the folder is named after, so the folder cannot exist before the analysis does. First every analysis.json under cv/, discarded/ and working/ is compared with the new one: a posting already applied to, discarded or still in flight is dropped with the earlier folder's path, and nothing is written. Otherwise jd.txt, analysis.json and approval_status.txt saying PENDING are written at once.

5 — The question is the only thing standing between you and the bill. Everything before it costs one or two small model calls; everything after it costs minutes of the large one. You are asked about every posting, whatever its should_apply says. Answer with the posting URL and it is stored in analysis.json (and in the spreadsheet); y submits without one; n or s files it under discarded/; q stops, and leaves the posting PENDING in working/. --yes answers for you, with the URL the analysis found if it found one.

6 — The CV is written in the background. Saying yes writes APPROVED and queues the folder; the CV thread takes one folder at a time, and the clipboard is read again at once, so you read the next posting while the last one's CV is written. Its lines are tagged with the folder's name, and held back while a question is on screen. q between postings lets the CV being written finish; the approved ones still queued stay in working/.

7 — The CV job is a session the client follows. POST /v1/cv returns 202 at once, under a session id that is the SHA-256 of the posting's text. The client then reads the session's events as the server writes them: each new step, printed; what each model call cost, printed; with -v, each step's detail too — what the step that just finished produced, and its token spend. Each step's result goes into the folder's steps/, as JSON, and every line the server logs for the job into log.log. The last event holds the document, the LaTeX and the PDF, and what the whole run cost; once those are written, the client acknowledges the session and the server deletes it.

If the connection drops, the client opens the stream again from the last event it got. If the client dies mid-job, the job does not: the server keeps writing the session. Run the same posting again and the server answers with the session it already has — replayed from the start, nothing paid twice. --new drops it and writes the CV again.

8 — The next start picks up where this one stopped. Anything left in working/ is offered back at startup: resume, clean or quit. Resume sends each folder where its own files say: APPROVED to the CV thread, PENDING to you before anything new is read, and a folder that already holds its document (cv_you_head_of_it.json) is posted to /v1/cv/render instead of starting a job — one LaTeX compile, no model call.

9 — Failure is filed, not printed and lost. A CV job that fails ends its session with an error event — the cause, and what the attempts cost — and everything the server logged for it is already in log.log; the client acknowledges the session and moves the job to error/. Any other call that fails carries a request_id, written into the log and printed: the server's own log has that request's lines under it.

10 — The spreadsheet is bookkeeping, never a reason to fail. A locked or broken applications.xlsx becomes a warning line in log.log; the CV was paid for and stays delivered.

docs.title: The CV pipeline
docs.text:
What POST /v1/cv does with the minutes it takes: six steps, each on a model of its own, then a render that trims the CV until it fits. The method is the one adapticv-ai worked out.

The code is server/src/cv_server/pipeline/cv_generator.py (CVGenerator, the steps as a LangGraph graph), cv_review.py (the validation loop) and cv_renderer.py (the compile and the page count).

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    START(["POST /v1/cv accepted<br/>202 + request_id"]) --> JD["<b>jd_evaluation</b><br/>the JD's key points, each with an importance"]
    JD -->|"Send, one per list"| SC["<b>profile_scoring</b><br/>one list of the profile against the key points"]
    SC --> MS["the scores into the profile<br/>text|3-80,7-40"]
    MS --> FS["<b>format_selection</b><br/>a format, the experiences, their duty caps"]
    FS -->|"Send"| WB["<b>cv</b><br/>the body"]
    FS -->|"Send, one per experience"| WD["<b>cv</b><br/>one experience"]
    WB --> CC["back in order"]
    WD --> CC
    CC -->|"Send"| VB["<b>validation</b><br/>the body, up to 5 rounds"]
    CC -->|"Send, one per experience"| VD["<b>validation</b><br/>one experience, up to 5 rounds"]
    VB --> CK["back in order"]
    VD --> CK
    CK --> HL["<b>highlight</b><br/>**bold** keywords, *italic* stacks"]
    HL --> R{"rendered:<br/>over the page limit?"}
    R -->|"yes, and a duty can go"| TRIM["remove the duty<br/>worth least"] --> R
    R -->|"no, or none can go"| FIN(["<b>result</b><br/>document · tex · pdf"])
Step Calls Shown Hands over jd_evaluation 1 the JD key_points: 6 to 15 requirements, each with keywords and an importance from 0 to 100 profile_scoring one per list of the profile — 9 for the example candidate the key points, one list, and its experience when the list is inside one scored_profile, score_reasons format_selection 1 the key points, the formats, the scored experiences format_selection: the format, the experiences shown, the duties of each, and why cv 1 for the body, 1 per experience shown the key points, the writing style, the schema, the scored profile or experience, its duty cap and its evidence cv_body, cv_experiences validation 1 to 5 per document the writing style, the round, the profile or the experience without scores, the generated text, the replacements that failed checked_body, checked_experiences highlight 1 the key points, the CV the models wrote, the evidence highlighted_resume

Each step has its own role in models.toml; cv and validation each serve two prompts, the body's and the experiences'. Each step's result is streamed to the client as it is ready, and stored beside the CV under steps/.

Scores. profile_scoring gives every item of the profile the key points it matches, at most four, each scored 0–100 for how completely the item proves it: a string becomes Led the migration.|3-80,7-40 (key point 3 at 80, key point 7 at 40), an object gets a "score": "3-80,7-40" field. The words that prove each match stay out of the profile, in score_reasons; the writer and the highlighter are shown them as EVIDENCE. The scores ride along to the end and come off at the render.

Coverage. A key point counts its two best duty scores, up to twice its importance (COVERAGE_BEST, COVERAGE_CAP): a duty on a key point already covered adds nothing, and weak matches cannot fill a key point before its strong ones. The duties prompt says the same in words, and the trim below uses the same rule.

Formats. What format_selection chooses from, and what the trim keeps:

Format Experiences Duties each Duties in all A 3 3–8 22 B 4 2–6 17 C 5 1–4 13

The code assumes nothing about the CV or the profile beyond the work experiences (each with an id and its duties), their duties and the writing_style: the prompts and the template decide everything else.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
A step that makes several calls fans them out with LangGraph's Send: one node per profile list, per experience, and they run at the same time. Each writes its answer, tagged with its position, into a list the graph collects; a node in code puts the answers back in profile order before the next step starts. The steps themselves run one after another.

The parallel nodes run in the job's own context, so their log lines and their token counts land in the job's session like any other. A call that fails — three unusable replies, an endpoint that refuses — fails the job with its own cause and stage, after the calls beside it have finished.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The validators check facts and grammar against your profile, with minimal edits; style is the writers' business. Each violation comes back as a call of a tool — replace_in_body or replace_in_duties — which is only a schema: the code applies the replacement, in the order the calls came, and asks again. A round with no call ends the review. A replacement whose text is not found goes back to the model as a FAILED REPLACEMENT. After five rounds (MAX_VALIDATIONS) the CV goes on with the last edits: a CV with a doubtful line in it is worth more to you than an error.

The validators count no pages. The page limit is the render's business alone.

docs.title: The render
docs.text:
After the highlight the CV is rendered — your candidate_data merged over the top, the scores removed — and its pages are counted. While it runs past the page limit (pages, 2 by default), one duty goes: of the experiences with more duties than the format's minimum, the duty whose removal loses the fewest coverage points; on a tie, the one with the lowest total score, then the older experience's. Then it is rendered again. When no duty can go, the longer CV is delivered.

Every render is of the merged document, so every page count is the page count of the CV you will send. That is why the endpoint takes candidate_data. No model is ever shown it: the highlighter sees what the models wrote, and your data goes over the top at the render, so a field a model invents can never replace a real name, email or address.

The renders before the last stay in the job's scratch directory. Only the final PDF is sent, in the result.

docs.title: Retries, budgets and what each failure costs
docs.text:
Guard Limit Set by On exhaustion Calls per model request (empty, cut off, or not the JSON asked for) 3 ATTEMPTS in models/selector.py 502 model_output, except for the highlight Highlight the same the same a warning; the CV is delivered unmarked Validation rounds per document 5 MAX_VALIDATIONS in pipeline/cv_review.py the CV goes on with the last edits Wall clock for the whole run 1200 s ATS_REQUEST_BUDGET_SECONDS 504 budget_exceeded, checked before each step One pdflatex compile 120 s ATS_LATEX_TIMEOUT 504 latex_timeout

A reply that is JSON is parsed and its type checked — a list or an object — and nothing more, as adapticv-ai does: no schema is enforced. A reply whose items do not line up with what was asked (fewer scores than items) fails the job.

docs.title: What the client sees while it runs
docs.text:
The job's session streams a status event as each step starts, with one line about the step that just finished: what it produced, and its tokens, thinking and time. Between them come an artifact event with each step's result, as the JSON it is, and the log and usage events that say what each model call did and cost.

{"status": "cv",
 "detail": "format A: experiences [0, 1, 2], duties [8, 8, 6], tokens used=4210, thinking=1952, elapsed=24.3s"}

The render belongs to the highlight step: it takes a second or a few.

The session ends with a result event — the document, its LaTeX and its PDF, and what the whole run cost — or, for a job that failed, an error event with the status and cause the work produced (502, 504, 422) and what it cost anyway. Either way it is the last thing the stream carries.

docs.title: Changing it for one request
docs.text:
Every prompt and both schemas the writer is shown can be replaced by a part of the same name: sys_prompt_jd_evaluation, sys_prompt_profile_scoring, sys_prompt_format_selection, sys_prompt_cv_body, cv_body_schema, sys_prompt_cv_duties, cv_duties_schema, sys_prompt_validation_body, sys_prompt_validation_duties, sys_prompt_highlight. So can the template and its images. The prompts and schemas are what the models read: editing one changes what they write.

Each step's model settings can be replaced too: <step>_extra_body, a JSON object, supersedes every setting models.toml gives that step — temperature, thinking, reasoning effort, the output cap, its own extra_body — and only the model, the endpoint and what you sent go out.

docs.title: What comes back
docs.text:
The result event's cv is {document, tex, pdf_base64}.

document is one flat object: what the models wrote, without the scores, with your candidate_data merged over the top. It has no schema of its own — what the template reads from it is between you and the template. Store it, edit it, and post it back to POST /v1/cv/render, which costs one LaTeX compile and no model call.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
render_document() is pure up to the compile: the document is escaped for LaTeX (including turning **bold** into \textbf{} and *italics* into \textit{}), generation_date is added — so re-rendering yesterday's file dates it today — and Jinja fills the template. The Jinja delimiters are LaTeX-safe: \VAR{}, \BLOCK{}, \#{}.

Images sent with the request are written next to the .tex under exactly the file name the part carried, because \includegraphics resolves relative to it. One pdflatex pass, not two: the shipped template has no \ref, \label or \tableofcontents, so a second pass would change nothing.

docs.title: The other three pipelines
docs.text:
None has a loop. Each runs on its own model: detect, analysis and letter.

  • jd_validator.detect — the free structural checks first (length band, no binary payload: static_jd_guess, shared with the client), and only if they pass does it cost one small model call.
  • jd_validator.analyze — extracts the posting's facts and scores it against your profile and your stated preferences. Up to three calls, the validation error fed back between them.
  • letter_generator.generate — prose in, prose out; 180–450 words, validated. The prompt asks the model to look the employer up when it can search the web; whether it can is the letter role's extra_body.

docs.title: Running the two halves apart
docs.text: ats-strike is deliberately two programs. This page is about where to put each one, and what the boundary buys you.

docs.title: Why they are separate
docs.text:
Client Server Holds your profile, contact data, template, images, the output tree the provider API key, the prompts, the LaTeX toolchain Costs to install one file ~780 MB of TeX Live Wants to be on the machine you copy postings on wherever compute is cheap and always on Scales by being copied being given more RAM and CPU

Splitting along that line is what makes each half simple:

  • The key never leaves the server. A client needs no provider account and no .env; the one secret it can hold is a bearer token for your own server.
  • Your data never rests on the server. The profile, the contact details, the preferences and the images arrive with each request and are thrown away when it ends. There is no database, no accounts, nothing to breach beyond the requests currently in flight.
  • Nobody installs LaTeX. The toolchain, its fonts and its failure modes live in one image you did not have to reproduce on Windows.
  • Each half changes on its own. The wire format is a third package both import; tests/test_architecture.py fails the build if either side imports the other. A new client mode touches no server code, and a new model role touches no client code.
flowchart LR
    subgraph c["client — your machine"]
        D["your data<br/><i>never uploaded, only sent</i>"]
    end
    subgraph w["contracts"]
        P["Envelope · CVStatus · RenderedCV<br/>JDAnalysis · static_jd_guess"]
    end
    subgraph s["server — a container"]
        K["MODEL_API_KEY<br/>prompts · template · pdflatex"]
    end
    c -->|"multipart"| s
    s -->|"JSON"| c
    c -.->|imports| w
    s -.->|imports| w

docs.title: Where to run each
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph A["1 — both on your laptop"]
        A1["cv"] -->|"localhost:8080"| A2["docker run ats-strike-server"]
    end
    subgraph B["2 — server on a box you own"]
        B1["cv on 2–3 machines"] -->|"private network"| B2["one container, one work dir"]
    end
    subgraph C["3 — server on a cloud platform"]
        C1["cv anywhere"] -->|"HTTPS + bearer token"| C2["one instance<br/>scale-to-zero is fine"]
    end

1 — Both local. The default. docker run -p 8080:8080 and server_url = "http://localhost:8080". No token needed: nothing but your own machine can reach it. This is also the cheapest way to try a different model — the container restarts in a second.

2 — Server on a machine you own. A NAS, a home server, a spare box. Set ATS_API_TOKEN even here: without it, anyone on the network can spend your provider credit. Point every client at it with server_url in cv.toml.

3 — Server on a cloud platform. Works as-is: the image runs as any uid, needs no volume, tolerates a read-only root filesystem, and answers /healthz for the platform probe without a token. Three things to get right:

  • Set ATS_API_TOKEN and put TLS in front. The client sends your profile and your contact details in the request body.
  • One instance per ATS_WORK_DIR, and WEB_CONCURRENCY=1. A running CV job lives in the process that started it, and a starting process closes every session it finds unfinished.
  • Scale-to-zero is fine, autoscaling is not. The client knocks on /healthz three times before its first real call, so a cold start is handled — but a stream that lands on another instance than the job's only sees the job if the work root is shared, and never sees it finish if that instance is new.
  • Give the work root a home that outlives the instance — a volume, or a bucket mounted as a folder — and a session survives the instance being recycled: the client gets its CV back by running the posting again. server/terraform mounts an OSS bucket on Alibaba Cloud. A platform that only gives CPU during requests (Cloud Run's default) stalls a job whenever no stream is open: give it CPU for the whole instance instead.

docs.title: What the client needs to know
docs.text:
Exactly three things, and only the first is required:

server_url = "https://ats-strike.example.run.app"
token      = "the-bearer-token"
timeout    = 1800          # how long to follow one CV job

or --server/--token, or ATS_API_URL/ATS_API_TOKEN. That is the entire coupling. Everything else the client sends is content.

docs.title: Keeping the boundary honest
docs.text:
If you change either half, these are the rules that keep them separable — they are also what the test suite checks:

  • client → contracts ← server. Neither side imports the other.
  • The contracts package imports pydantic and nothing else. It is loaded by a web server and by a frozen executable, and has to stay cheap in both.
  • No server-side dependency reaches the client: no openai, no jinja2, no pypdf, no fastapi. subprocess is allowed in exactly one file — the clipboard helper probe.
  • Anything new on the wire goes in contracts/, not in a client-side model that happens to match.

docs.title: Should the repository be split too?
docs.text:
The artifacts are already independent — a container image and an executable, built by separate CI jobs from disjoint directories. What is shared is the repository, the lock file and the version number.

Keeping one repository is the better trade today:

  • cv_contracts is imported by both halves as a workspace member. Two repositories would mean publishing it to an index, or vendoring it twice, to buy nothing a directory boundary does not already give.
  • A wire change currently lands as one commit that updates both sides and one test run that proves they still agree — tests/test_integration.py drives the real client against the real server app in-process. Split, that becomes a release dance across three repositories.
  • Both halves are small. The reason to split a repository is that two teams keep colliding in it; nothing here collides.

Split it when one of these becomes true, and not before: the client acquires its own release cadence and users who never touch the server; someone else's client needs cv_contracts from an index; or the server grows a private deployment history that should not be in a public client repository. When that day comes, the seam is already cut — publish contracts/ as a versioned package, pin it from both sides, and move the two directories out.

docs.title: Developing locally, in VS Code
docs.text:
This page is for working on ats-strike itself: both halves on your own machine, under the debugger, breakpoints on either side of the HTTP call. No container, no cloud instance — the client's server_url is localhost, and if you point the server at a local model endpoint too, nothing leaves the machine at all.

It is the same topology as "both on your laptop" in the deployment page, swapping docker run for uv run so you get a debugger instead of an image.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Python 3.12+, uv Builds the workspace's one .venv for all three packages VS Code with the Python extension Ships debugpy, which the launch configs below use pdflatex on PATH Only for /v1/cv and /v1/cv/render to actually produce a PDF — see below A model endpoint Your own provider key, or a local one — see Configure

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv sync

One .venv at the repository root for contracts/, server/ and client/. Point VS Code's Python interpreter at ${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python if it does not pick it up on its own.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env

Fill in MODEL_API_KEY and MODEL_BASE_URL for the provider you use — see the "API keys" section of the repository's server/README.md. cv_server loads .env itself (python-dotenv), so nothing in launch.json needs to pass it along.

Leave ATS_API_TOKEN unset. That is fine here for the same reason it is fine in deployment's scenario 1: nothing but your own machine can reach localhost:8080.

For a stack that makes no outbound network call at all, point the server at a local model server instead of a hosted provider:

MODEL_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
MODEL_API_KEY=anything   # Ollama ignores it, but the OpenAI client requires one

docs.title: The launch configs
docs.text:
.vscode/launch.json has:

Name Runs server (ats-strike) cv_server.server:main in-process — the same entry point as uv run ats-strike, just under debugpy client (submit-raw) cv submit-raw examples/posting.txt against the example candidate in examples/candidate/ — one CV, no clipboard, no confirmation prompt. The quickest way to prove the two halves talk to each other client (clipboard) The interactive mode, against the same example data

and one compound, server + client (clipboard), that starts both. Each runs as its own debugpy session, so a breakpoint in cv_server and one in cv_client both work at the same time — they are two processes, not one call stack, so stepping through one will not show you the other side of the HTTP request.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
1. Set the Run and Debug target to server + client (clipboard) and press F5. Two debug sessions start; wait for the server's Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8080 in its Debug Console before copying a posting.
  2. Copy the text of the repository's examples/posting.txt (or any real one). The client asks whether to submit; say y. Output lands under ats-strike-data/dev/.
  3. To check just the wiring without touching the clipboard, run client (submit-raw) on its own against an already-running server — it needs no confirmation and exits when done, which is also the one that works over an SSH or container remote with no clipboard to read.

Breakpoints in cv_server/api/ catch a request as it arrives; breakpoints in cv_client/ catch it being built or the response being parsed. curl localhost:8080/healthz works the whole time, from either a terminal or the client's own startup check.

docs.title: pdflatex, without the container
docs.text:
The image installs a specific, minimal set so the CV compiles and its icons render — see the Dockerfile at the repository root. Reproduce it on the host:

Platform What to install Debian/Ubuntu sudo apt install texlive-latex-base cm-super, then sudo server/docker/install-fontawesome5.sh server/docker/vendor/fontawesome5.tar.xz for the contact icons (see server/docker/vendor/README.md) macOS A full MacTeX install already includes fontawesome5; nothing to vendor Windows MiKTeX with "install packages on the fly" on — the first compile pulls what it needs

Confirm with kpsewhich fontawesome5.sty (prints a path) and curl localhost:8080/healthz ("pdflatex": true). Without it, everything except /v1/cv and /v1/cv/render still works — /v1/jd/detect and /v1/jd/analysis never touch LaTeX.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see What to do ModuleNotFoundError: cv_client / cv_server VS Code is using a different interpreter than .venv. Reselect it, or re-run uv sync cannot reach the ats-strike server at http://localhost:8080 The server (ats-strike) session is not running, or is still starting — check its Debug Console "status": "degraded" from /healthz No pdflatex on PATH; see above no clipboard here: neither DISPLAY nor WAYLAND_DISPLAY… apt install xclip (X11) or wl-clipboard (Wayland) locally, or a devcontainer/SSH remote with no display at all — use client (submit-raw) instead RuntimeError: ... is not set. Set it in your .env MODEL_API_KEY is empty in .env at the repository root address already in use on :8080 Something else is already listening — a leftover docker run, most likely. Stop it, or set PORT before starting the server config

docs.title: Building these pages
docs.text:
The site is doc/ rendered by MkDocs with the Material theme, configured in mkdocs.yml at the repository root. Both are pinned in the docs dependency group of pyproject.toml, so they come with the workspace and not from your system Python:

uv run --group docs mkdocs serve    # live preview on http://localhost:8000
uv run --group docs mkdocs build    # static HTML into site/ (gitignored)
Supported MkDocs 1.6+ with mkdocs-material 9.5+ Not supported MkDocs 2.0, which removes the plugin system Material is built on. Both are capped in pyproject.toml Diagrams Mermaid, as ```mermaid fences, rendered by Material through pymdownx.superfences. A different theme will print them as code Strictness strict: true — a link to a page or an anchor that does not exist fails the build

To add a page: put the Markdown in doc/ and add it to the nav: in mkdocs.yml. A page that is not in the nav still builds, but nothing links to it.

The published site is versioned. Each release deploys its own copy with mike, and the selector in the header switches between them — so the docs you are reading match the version you downloaded, not whatever main says today. Locally you still just run mkdocs; the version selector is the one thing that will not appear, because it is built from a versions.json that only exists on the published site. See Cutting a release.

docs.title: Model configurations
docs.text:
A running ledger of which provider, model and role combinations have been tried, and what happened. models.toml says what is shipped; this page says what is known to work, and why the rest does not.

Update it whenever a role changes model or provider, or a provider surprises you. An entry is only works if a real run finished and its output was used. A failure is recorded with its cause when the cause is known, and with the exact error name when it is not.

Status Meaning works A real run finished and its output was used fails It was tried and failed; the cause is in the notes unconfirmed Configured, but no run has been recorded yet

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: What each endpoint is known to accept. This is the part that carries over to the next model you try.

docs.title: Alibaba Model Studio (DashScope): Qwen and hosted DeepSeek

Endpoint: https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1, or the workspace endpoint of the same form shown in the console.

docs.text: Add a row under the role, with the provider, the exact model id, the settings that differ from models.toml (including any ATS_<ROLE>_* override), the date and the outcome. For a failure, the error name from the job log (provider_error: … PermissionDeniedError) or the server's own line for it (a CV's log.log carries every one) belongs in the notes; the cause belongs there once it is known. docs.title: The HTTP API
docs.text:
Everything is multipart/form-data in and JSON out. There is no database and no accounts: every request carries what it needs. The one thing the server keeps is a CV job's session — the events it streams — until the client says it has everything, or until it is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS.

Base URL is wherever you run it — http://localhost:8080 by default. The interactive OpenAPI page FastAPI generates is at /docs.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Parts. Every text part can be sent as a file (-F jd=@JD.txt) or as a plain field (-F jd_text=...); the file wins if you send both. JSON parts (candidate_profile, candidate_data, document, analysis) must be files, must parse, and must be JSON objects. A UTF-8 BOM is stripped. Any single part over ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES (2 MB) is refused with 413 before it is read.

Images. The images part is repeatable, at most 10 per request. Each part's file name is the name the template includes it under — that is the whole interface. Path components are stripped.

Auth. If ATS_API_TOKEN is set, every /v1/... call must send Authorization: Bearer <token>; /healthz stays open so a platform probe works. With no token set, the server is open to anyone who can reach it, which is only reasonable on a private network.

The envelope. Every response, success or failure, has the same shape:

{
  "request_id": "b510f8dff047",   // also in the X-Request-Id header
  "ok": true,
  "data": { },                    // the payload, when ok
  "error": null                   // one line, when not
}

Fields that are null are omitted. Nothing else rides on a reply. What the server did — every line it logged, every model call and its cost — is streamed by a CV job as events; for any other request it is in the server's own log, under the request id.

Request ids. The server generates a 12-hex-character id per request and echoes it in the X-Request-Id header. An inbound X-Request-Id is honoured if it matches [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}. For POST /v1/cv it is the session's id, and names its directory under the work root, so anything else would be a way to write where the server was not asked to.

docs.title: POST /v1/jd/detect
docs.text:
Is this text a job posting?

curl -F jd=@JD.txt localhost:8080/v1/jd/detect
Part jd / jd_text required The text to check

Structural checks run first — length band (ATS_JD_MIN_CHARS … _MAX_CHARS, 500–30000 by default), no binary payload — and only if they pass does it cost one small model call. The answer is {"is_job_description": true|false}; why it was rejected is in the request's log, not in the reply. The same structural check ships in cv_contracts.static_jd_guess, so a client can run it before spending the call at all.

docs.title: POST /v1/jd/analysis
docs.text:
Scores a posting against your profile and extracts its facts.

curl -F jd=@JD.txt \
     -F candidate_profile=@candidate_profile.json \
     -F pers_preferences=@candidate_preferences.md \
     localhost:8080/v1/jd/analysis
Part jd / jd_text required The posting candidate_profile required JSON object: everything you have done pers_preferences / pers_preferences_text required What you want from a job, in prose sys_prompt_analysis optional Replace the analysis prompt analysis_extra_body optional JSON object: the analysis model's settings for this request, instead of models.toml's (see POST /v1/cv)

Returns a JDAnalysis:

Field Type match_percentage int 0–100, how well the posting fits the profile match_rationale str? One line saying why job_title str As extracted from the posting work_location str? e.g. "Milan, Italy" work_mode str full_remote | hybrid | on_site | not_specified expected_salary str? As stated, e.g. "EUR 60k-80k" max_salary int Upper bound, or -1 if not found salary_match bool? Whether the JD's salary meets your preferences; null if the JD states none hard_skills, soft_skills str[] Up to 4 each company_name str The employer, or the agency posting_url str? If the posting text carries one gaps str Where you fall short of the posting pers_preferences str How the posting reads against your preferences pers_preference_score float The summed score of the preferences it satisfies should_apply str NO (skip) | CHECK (human check) | YES (apply) — per the should_apply rules in your preferences, else salary_match should_apply_reason str Why should apply company_evaluation str?
