docs.title: POST /v1/cv → GET /v1/cv/{id}/events → DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
docs.text:
The expensive one: minutes of model calls. It does not wait. It starts the job as a session, which the caller follows as a stream of server-sent events and lets go of once it has stored the CV.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as caller
    participant S as server
    C->>S: POST /v1/cv (jd, profile, candidate_data, …)<br/>X-Request-Id: the session id
    S-->>C: 202 {reattached: false}
    C->>S: GET /v1/cv/{id}/events
    loop while the job runs
        S-->>C: status · artifact · log · usage
    end
    S-->>C: result {cv, detail, total} — and the stream closes
    Note over C: stores the CV
    C->>S: DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
    S-->>C: 200
ID=$(sha256sum JD.txt | cut -c1-64)
curl -s -H "X-Request-Id: $ID" -F jd=@JD.txt \
     -F candidate_profile=@candidate_profile.json \
     -F candidate_data=@candidate_data.json localhost:8080/v1/cv
curl -sN localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID/events      # the job, to its last event
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID    # once the CV is saved

docs.title: POST /v1/cv
docs.text:
Part jd / jd_text required The posting candidate_profile required JSON object — what the model tailors from candidate_data required JSON object — what the template prints sys_prompt_jd_evaluation, sys_prompt_profile_scoring, sys_prompt_format_selection, sys_prompt_cv_body, sys_prompt_cv_duties, sys_prompt_validation_body, sys_prompt_validation_duties, sys_prompt_highlight optional Replace a step's prompt for this request cv_body_schema, cv_duties_schema optional Replace the JSON schema the writer is shown for the body, or for an experience template optional Replace resume.tex.jinja, page counts included images optional Repeatable, ≤10. Each part's file name is the name the template includes it under. jd_evaluation_extra_body, profile_scoring_extra_body, format_selection_extra_body, cv_extra_body, validation_extra_body, highlight_extra_body optional JSON object: that step's model settings for this request (see below) pages optional Page limit the CV must fit. Default 2, minimum 1.

<role>_extra_body is a form field holding a JSON object, sent into the request body as is. It supersedes every setting models.toml gives that role — temperature, the thinking switch, reasoning effort, the output cap, its own extra_body: besides the model and the messages, what you sent is all that goes out ({"temperature": 0.7, "top_p": 0.9}, {"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}}, …). The endpoint and the provider stay. A field that is not a JSON object is a 400. An endpoint ignores the fields for roles it does not have, so a client may send all of its own with every request. detect takes none.

Answers 202 with {"request_id": "<id>", "ok": true, "data": {"reattached": false}}.

The session id is the caller's. Send it as X-Request-Id. The client uses the SHA-256 of the posting's text, so running the same posting again finds the session it already has, and a client that died, or lost its connection, loses nothing it paid for. When the id already has a session, nothing is started — no slot is claimed either — and the answer says "reattached": true: follow its events as for a new one. Sessions whose last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS (1 by default) are deleted first, so an old one is not found. With no X-Request-Id, the server picks an id and every POST is a new job. 429 too_many_jobs applies to a new job only.

Why candidate_data is required. The page limit is enforced by actually compiling the CV and counting its pages, trimming duties until it fits. A page count taken with the contact block missing is not the page count of the CV you will send. No model is shown candidate_data: it goes to the renderer and nowhere else.

docs.title: GET /v1/cv/{id}/events
docs.text:
text/event-stream. Every event the session has — from the first, or from the one after Last-Event-ID: n — then each new one as the job writes it, until the last, after which the stream closes. A : ping line every 15 quiet seconds keeps the connection open through a long model call. The session is files, so a stream can be opened as often as you like, while the job runs or long after, and a dropped one loses nothing: reconnect with the last id: you got.

id: 1
event: status
data: {"status": "jd_evaluation", "detail": ""}

id: 2
event: log
data: {"ts": "2026-01-15T09:30:53Z", "level": "INFO", "stage": "cv.jd_evaluation", "message": "  ⏱ [jd_evaluation] deepseek-flash 21.2s | input=1847, thinking=7256, output=832, …"}

id: 3
event: usage
data: {"role": "jd_evaluation", "model": "deepseek-flash", "seconds": 21.2, "input_tokens": 1847, "thinking_tokens": 7256, "output_tokens": 832}

id: 4
event: artifact
data: {"name": "key_points", "data": [{"id": 1, "requirement": "Engineering manager", "keywords": ["Engineering Manager"], "importance": 100}, …]}

id: 5
event: status
data: {"status": "profile_scoring", "detail": "11 key points, tokens used=9935, thinking=7256, elapsed=21.3s"}

id: 97
event: result
data: {"cv": {"document": {…}, "tex": "\\documentclass…", "pdf_base64": "JVBERi0…"}, "detail": "done, 21 model calls, …", "total": {"calls": 21, "seconds": 961.4, …}}
Event Payload When status CVStatus: status, detail Each step: jd_evaluation, profile_scoring, format_selection, cv, validation, highlight artifact CVArtifact: name, data Each step's result as it is ready: key_points, scored_profile, score_reasons, format_selection, cv_body, cv_experiences, checked_body, checked_experiences, highlighted_resume log LogEntry: ts, level, stage, message Every line the server logged for the job (at most 2000) usage ModelCall: role, model, seconds, input_tokens, thinking_tokens, output_tokens After every model call, failed attempts included result CVResult: cv, detail, total The job is done: the last event error CVFailure: http_status, error, total The job failed: the last event

detail is written for a person: what the step that just finished produced, and what it cost. An artifact is JSON, not a file: the client stores each one as it likes — the ats-strike client as steps/<name>.json beside the CV. No PDF is ever an artifact; the only one sent is the result's. total adds up every model call of the run, so a failed job still says what it cost.

A failed job reports itself here, with the status its cause maps to (502, 504, 422) and the cause in the same form as any other error. A job the server restarted under ends with 503 unavailable. See the CV pipeline for what each step does.

cv.document is one flat object — what the models wrote with your candidate_data merged over the top, so a field a model invents can never replace a real contact detail. It has no schema: what the template reads from it is between you and the template. Store it, edit it, post it back to /v1/cv/render.

404 unknown_request means there is no session by that id: it was acknowledged, it is older than the server keeps sessions, or it never started.

docs.title: DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
docs.text: Acknowledge: the caller has everything, and the server deletes the session. Do it once the CV is stored, not before — until then the session is what lets a caller that died get its CV back for nothing. 409 job_not_ready while the job runs: its worker is still writing there, and a new session for the same posting would be the same directory. 404 when there is no such session.

docs.title: DELETE /v1/cv?all
docs.text: Deletes every session whose job is not running, and answers {"deleted": 3, "running": 1}. Without all it is a 400: not something to do by accident.

docs.title: POST /v1/cv/render
docs.text:
curl -F document=@cv.json     localhost:8080/v1/cv/render
curl -F tex=@cv_edited.tex    localhost:8080/v1/cv/render
Part document one of the two A CV document as JSON — a CV job's cv.document, or anything else your template can read tex one of the two Ready LaTeX, compiled as-is template optional Replace resume.tex.jinja images optional Repeatable, ≤10

Sending both, or neither, is a 400. Returns {tex, pdf_base64}; document is not echoed back, because whoever asked for the render already has it. Cheap and deterministic: editing the content and re-rendering never costs a model call.

The rendered .tex is dated at render time, so re-rendering yesterday's document dates it today.

docs.title: POST /v1/letter
docs.text:
curl -F jd=@JD.txt -F candidate_profile=@candidate_profile.json \
     -F candidate_data=@candidate_data.json \
     -F analysis=@analysis.json localhost:8080/v1/letter
Part jd / jd_text required The posting candidate_profile required JSON object candidate_data required JSON object — the header block's name, email, phone, LinkedIn analysis optional A JDAnalysis — makes the letter more targeted, and enables the web research sys_prompt_letter optional Replace the letter prompt letter_extra_body optional JSON object: the letter model's settings for this request, instead of models.toml's — a web search it had there goes too, unless you send it again

Returns {"text": "…", "words": 312}, validated between 180 and 450 words. When the analysis names the employer and the endpoint supports server-side web search, the model is told to research the company; an endpoint that rejects the flag falls back to writing without it.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed request returns the same envelope with ok: false and one line saying what went wrong, its kind and its stage — one line, except that a failed compile adds the end of the TeX log on the lines after it, because only the TeX log says where the document breaks:

{"request_id": "b510f8dff047", "ok": false,
 "error": "model_output [cv.profile_scoring]: profile_scoring: no usable reply in 3 attempts:\n- it is not a JSON list"}
Status Kind Means 400 bad_request, missing_part, bad_part A required part is absent, empty, not UTF-8, not JSON, not an object, or mutually exclusive parts were both sent 401 unauthorized ATS_API_TOKEN is set and the request had no matching token. Answers with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer 404 unknown_request No CV session by that id: acknowledged, older than the server keeps sessions, or never started 409 job_not_ready The CV job is still running, so its session cannot be acknowledged yet 413 part_too_large A part exceeded ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES 422 latex_compile The template or the .tex does not compile. The end of the TeX log follows the error line 422 validation_error An uploaded document does not match the expected schema 429 too_many_jobs All job slots are busy. Answers with Retry-After: 30 502 model_output The model never produced usable output within the attempts allowed 502 provider_error, provider_unreachable The model endpoint failed. The body is never echoed — it can carry the endpoint and the key 504 latex_timeout, budget_exceeded, provider_timeout A compile, the whole run, or the provider hit its timeout 500 internal_error A bug here. Everything else above is an answer, not a crash

The stage in brackets ([cv.profile_scoring], [compile], [render]) says where in the pipeline it happened. For a CV job, the attempts that led there — every failed one included, with its token cost — are in the session's log and usage events. For any other request, the server's own log (stdout) has every line under the request id.

docs.title: The wire format as a package
docs.text:
cv_contracts is the same set of pydantic models the server answers with, published as its own package so a client can import it instead of hand-rolling the shapes:

from cv_contracts import (
    Envelope, CVStatus, RenderedCV, CoverLetter, ServerStatus,
    JDAnalysis, JDDetection, LogEntry, static_jd_guess,
    EVENT_PAYLOADS, CVArtifact, CVResult, CVFailure, CVSession, ModelCall, TokenUsage,
)

envelope = Envelope[RenderedCV].model_validate(response.json())
pdf_bytes = envelope.data.pdf_bytes()          # decodes pdf_base64

result = EVENT_PAYLOADS["result"].model_validate_json(data)   # a result event's data

It depends on pydantic and nothing else. The CV document itself deliberately has no model there: it is whatever the models wrote merged with whatever your candidate_data.json holds, and only your LaTeX template has an opinion about it.

docs.title: Cutting a release
docs.text:
One version for the whole repository, and one thing you type. Actions → Release → Run workflow → 0.3.0 → Run. Nothing happens on your machine.

.github/workflows/release.yml writes that number into the three pyproject.toml files and uv.lock, commits it, tags v0.3.0, and builds everything from that tag: .tar.gz and .zip archives on the release page, the server image on Docker Hub, and this site under its own version.

docs.title: Before the first one
docs.text:
Two repository secrets, set once under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

Secret What it is DOCKERHUB_USERNAME The Docker Hub account that owns lmstch/ats-strike. DOCKERHUB_TOKEN An access token for it, not the account password.

Without them the image job fails at docker login, after the image has been built and checked — and because package waits on every job, no release is published until they exist.

GitHub Pages, once, under Settings → Pages: source GitHub Actions. Not Deploy from a branch — gh-pages is still where every version is kept, but the docs job uploads that branch and deploys it itself. Choosing the branch instead hands publishing to the build Pages runs on a push, and that build never fires here: mike pushes as github-actions[bot], and a GITHUB_TOKEN push starts no workflow run. The branch would move and the site would not. Nothing else writes that branch — it belongs to mike.

One consequence worth knowing: with this source, pushing gh-pages by hand publishes nothing. A mike deploy --push from a laptop updates the store and leaves the site where it was. Releasing is what publishes.

The workflow also declares permissions: contents: write. The repository default for GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only, and this workflow pushes a commit, a tag and a release; without that block the push is refused with a 403. The docs job asks for two more of its own — pages: write and id-token: write — because it deploys the site rather than leaving that to a branch build.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Type the number bare: 0.3.0, not v0.3.0. The tag gets the v.

It refuses, before writing anything, when:

Refusal Why the version is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH the tag, the archive name and the image tag are all built from it you dispatched from a branch other than main a release that is not on the main line is a release nobody can reconstruct v<version> is already on the remote re-releasing a version silently is how two different binaries end up with one number

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    TAG["<b>tag</b><br/>validate · rewrite three pyprojects<br/>uv lock · commit · tag · push --atomic"]
    B1["<b>build</b> — ubuntu<br/>pyinstaller → cv<br/>assert <i>cv version</i>"]
    B2["<b>build</b> — windows<br/>pyinstaller → cv.exe<br/>assert <i>cv version</i>"]
    IMG["<b>image</b><br/>DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build<br/>assert /healthz version<br/>docker push :x.y.z and :latest"]
    DOC["<b>docs</b><br/>mike deploy x.y.z latest<br/>mike set-default latest<br/>→ gh-pages → deploy-pages"]
    PKG["<b>package</b><br/>download both binaries<br/>assemble · tar.gz<br/>gh release create"]
    TAG --> B1 --> PKG
    TAG --> B2 --> PKG
    TAG --> IMG --> PKG
    TAG --> DOC --> PKG

The tag is pushed first, before anything is built. That order is forced: the binaries have to carry the version, so the bump has to precede the build, and the build jobs can only check out a commit that exists on the remote. Every "tag last" arrangement ends up shipping the bump as a patch and re-applying it in three jobs — more moving parts for the same result.

package waits for every other job, so the release page never announces a version whose server image is not on Docker Hub or whose docs are not up. The image job logs in to the registry after the build and the health check, so a broken image never gets as far as authenticating.

docs.title: Where the version lives
docs.text:
There is no __version__ string in the source to forget to bump. One number is written in one place and everything else reads it:

Where Who writes it contracts/, server/, client/ pyproject.toml the workflow, with sed uv.lock uv lock, in the same commit cv version, and every --verbose run importlib.metadata.version("ats-strike-client") /healthz and the OpenAPI document importlib.metadata.version("ats-strike-server")

uv.lock is in that list because it records each workspace member's version as well. A bump that did not regenerate it would commit a lock that disagrees with the manifests, which uv lock --check and uv sync --locked both refuse. The binaries themselves would still be right — uv sync --frozen builds the workspace members from source, so the manifest wins — but a repository whose lock contradicts its manifests is a trap for the next person.

What guards the version in the artefacts is not the lock but the assertions: both build jobs run cv version on the binary they just produced, and the image job reads /healthz from the container it just built, before any of it is published.

docs.title: What gets published
docs.text:
Artifact Where Name both executables and the files beside them the release page ats-strike-x.y.z.tar.gz and ats-strike-x.y.z.zip the server image Docker Hub lmstch/ats-strike:x.y.z and :latest this site GitHub Pages, from gh-pages /x.y.z/, and /latest/ which / redirects to

The archive is flat on purpose:

cv                           the Linux executable, already +x
cv.exe                       the Windows executable
README.md                    the client README, links rewritten for this layout
cv.toml                 points at http://localhost:8080; edit it
candidate_profile.json       the fictional set, ready to edit
candidate_data.json
candidate_preferences.md
candidate_signature.png
posting.txt                  something to try it on

The client looks for its files by name in the folder you run it in — see discovery.py — so a flat archive is a working folder as soon as it is extracted. There is nothing to move and no config to rename:

mkdir ats-strike && tar xzf ats-strike-0.3.0.tar.gz -C ats-strike
cd ats-strike
./cv submit-raw posting.txt --server https://your-server

Extract it into a folder of its own, as above. A flat archive unpacks nine files wherever you stand.

docs.title: The site's own versions
docs.text:
mike keeps one built copy of doc/ per release on the gh-pages branch, plus a versions.json that the selector in the header reads:

gh-pages/
├── 0.2.0/           one full site per release
├── 0.3.0/
├── latest/          an alias, moved by --update-aliases
├── versions.json    what the selector offers
└── index.html       redirects / to latest/

The docs version is the release version, in full — 0.3.0, not 0.3. mike's own convention is major.minor, so that patches share a docs version, but one number for the whole repository is worth more here than a shorter selector: a tag, an archive, an image tag and a docs URL that all read 0.3.0 need no explaining.

mike set-default --push latest runs on every release. It is idempotent, and doing it every time is what lets the first release set the redirect up with no manual step.

Locally, mkdocs serve and mkdocs build are unchanged and unversioned. The selector is built at runtime from a versions.json that only the published site has, so it will not appear in a local preview — that is expected, not a misconfiguration.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
What failed What is left behind What to do tag nothing — the branch and the tag are pushed with --atomic, so they land together or not at all fix it and dispatch again a later job, transiently — a runner flake, a registry 5xx the bump commit and the tag, no release Re-run failed jobs. tag is skipped and its sha output carries over, so the re-run builds the same commit. a later job, for a real reason — the Windows build broke, the image fails its health check, a doc link is dead the same the release was never valid. Fix it on main and release the next patch number.

docs and image both publish before package does, so a failure after them can leave a site and an image for a version that has no release page. Both are safe to redo: mike deploy overwrites the version's directory, and docker push overwrites the tag.

The last row is the one that looks wrong and is not. Tags are free, a skipped patch number costs nothing, and the alternative — teaching the workflow to delete and re-push its own tag — is a feature nobody asked for that can destroy a good release.

One thing worth knowing: the release commit does not run CI. Pushes made with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger further workflow runs. Its only difference from main is three version strings and the lock, and both uv sync --frozen and the Docker build fail loudly on a broken lock — but the rule that follows from it is: release only from a green main.
